lab_title: Apparent Retrograde Motion: Mars on the Move
top_level_objectives: Observe and describe the apparent retrograde motion of Mars as seen from Earth against the background stars.
Compare the historical geocentric (epicycle) explanation for retrograde motion with the modern heliocentric model.
Explain how the relative orbital speeds and positions of Earth and Mars cause the illusion of retrograde motion.
Predict how the characteristics of retrograde motion change for more distant planets like Jupiter and Saturn.

scenes.brief_purpose: To introduce the phenomenon of apparent retrograde motion by showing Mars's path across the night sky over several months.
key_visuals: A photorealistic night sky with familiar constellations.
A bright, reddish point of light representing Mars.
A glowing trail that traces Mars's path over time, clearly showing the S-shaped retrograde loop.
student_actions: Initiate a time-lapse animation to watch Mars's path unfold against the background stars.
Identify the points where Mars appears to slow down, reverse direction (retrograde), and then resume its normal eastward (prograde) motion.

scenes.brief_purpose: To demonstrate the historical, Earth-centered explanation for retrograde motion using Ptolemy's system of deferents and epicycles.
key_visuals: A stylized model of the solar system with a static Earth at the center.
Mars orbiting the Earth on a large circle (the deferent).
A smaller circle (the epicycle) attached to the deferent, on which Mars itself moves.
student_actions: Play an animation of the geocentric model to observe how the combined motion of the deferent and epicycle creates a looping path.
Recognize the complexity and contrived nature of the epicycle model required to explain the observed motion.

scenes.brief_purpose: To introduce the modern, heliocentric model as a simpler alternative and set the stage for the correct explanation.
key_visuals: A 3D model of the inner solar system with the Sun at the center.
The orbital paths of Earth and Mars clearly depicted.
Labels for the Sun, Earth, and Mars.
student_actions: Explore the 3D model of the heliocentric system from any angle.
Identify the key components and note that Earth is on a smaller, inner orbit compared to Mars.

scenes.brief_purpose: To provide the core explanation for retrograde motion: that it's an illusion created when faster-moving Earth overtakes slower-moving Mars.
key_visuals: The animated heliocentric model from a 'top-down' perspective.
A persistent line-of-sight vector extending from Earth, through Mars, to a distant plane representing the background constellations.
A marker on the background plane that traces the apparent position of Mars.
student_actions: Use a time slider to control the orbits of Earth and Mars.
Observe how the line of sight sweeps backward against the stars as Earth passes Mars, creating the apparent retrograde loop.
Pinpoint the moments of opposition, when Earth is directly between the Sun and Mars, which corresponds to the middle of the retrograde loop.

scenes.brief_purpose: To generalize the concept by comparing Mars's retrograde motion to that of a more distant planet, Jupiter.
key_visuals: The heliocentric model expanded to include Jupiter and its orbit.
Simultaneous animations of Earth overtaking both Mars and Jupiter.
Distinct visual trails showing the separate retrograde loops for both planets against the background stars.
student_actions: Observe the animations of both planets' retrograde motions.
Compare the size, duration, and frequency of Jupiter's retrograde loop to Mars's loop.
Conclude that more distant planets have smaller and less frequent retrograde loops because the parallax effect from Earth's motion is less pronounced.

scenes.brief_purpose: To synthesize the lab's concepts by showing the Earth-based view and the heliocentric view side-by-side.
key_visuals: On one side, the time-lapse of Mars's loop in the night sky from Scene 1.
On the other side, the animated 'overtaking' model from Scene 4.
The two animations are synchronized in time.
student_actions: Watch the synchronized animations to directly connect the cause (Earth overtaking Mars) with the effect (the apparent backward motion).
Answer a series of concluding questions to assess understanding of the relationship between the two perspectives.
